books.name: I Would Prefer Not To
books.why: A 170-year line of people who simply stop cooperating, first as fiction, then as an argument about work.

stops.step: The founding refusal: a copyist who answers every request with "I would prefer not to" and never says why.
Six years later Russia produces a whole novel of a man who won't get off the couch; "Oblomovism" became a political word.
Five years after that, the refusal gets a philosophy: the Underground Man won't even agree that two plus two makes four.
The refusal moves inside a starving writer's head; Hamsun read Dostoevsky closely, and Kafka read Hamsun.
Bukowski named Hamsun among his gods. Factotum is Hunger in Los Angeles: job after job, quit or fired, and funny about it.
Russell makes the same case with a straight face: a four-hour workday and the moral cost of overwork.
Ninety years on, the data: a lot of people already do nothing at work and are miserable pretending otherwise. Bartleby was early.

books.name: The Eternal Return
books.why: Nietzsche's thought experiment (would you live this exact life again, forever?) keeps getting turned into novels, and it ends up back at Vonnegut.

stops.step: Start at Zarathustra's "On the Vision and the Riddle": the gateway called Moment, and the dwarf who says time is a circle.
Ouspensky makes the idea into a plot: a man gets to relive his life and watches himself make every mistake again.
Kundera opens his novel by arguing with Nietzsche: if we only live once, nothing weighs anything.
The pulp version: a man dies at 43 and wakes up at 18, again and again. Groundhog Day before Groundhog Day.
Atkinson puts Nietzsche's demon from The Gay Science in the epigraph and lets Ursula die and restart until she gets the century right.
Vonnegut's last novel: everyone has to relive ten years on autopilot. The joke is that we were never steering anyway. So it goes.

books.name: The Author Walks In
books.why: The comic novel that knows it is a novel, from Cervantes to the moment Vonnegut sits down at the bar in Midland City.

stops.step: In Part Two the characters have read Part One and complain about it. Everything after this is a footnote.
Sterne takes Cervantes as patron saint and writes a life that never gets past the narrator's birth; black pages, squiggle diagrams.
Diderot lifts a whole episode from Sterne and adds the argument I care about: a servant who believes everything is "written up above" while his author keeps interrupting him.
Characters revolt against the novelist who invented them and drug him so they can live their own lives.
Barth turns the trick into an American theory of fiction: the story about the story about the story.
Vonnegut walks into his own book, sits in the cocktail lounge, and sets Kilgore Trout free. The most tender use of the trick.

books.name: Books Made of Books
books.why: The library as labyrinth, trap and fire: novels built out of imaginary books, commentaries and archives.

stops.step: A sinologist who loves his library more than any person, and burns with it. The dark side of my whole project.
Nine years later the library becomes the universe ("The Library of Babel") and the encyclopedia invents a planet ("Tlön").
A 999-line poem swallowed by a mad commentator's notes; Borges's fake scholarship turned into a whole novel.
Eco names his blind librarian Jorge of Burgos and burns the library at the end, Canetti's ending at monastery scale.
A novel written as three rival encyclopedias, sold in male and female editions that differ by one paragraph.
Footnotes on a documentary that may not exist, about a house bigger inside than out: the commentary eats the text.

stops.t: The Secret History of Twin Peaks
stops.step: The same form in a pop key: a town told as a found dossier, annotated by the agents reading it.

books.name: Out of Gogol's Overcoat
books.why: A teacher-and-student line from Gogol's clerk to the Iowa workshop where Vonnegut taught John Irving.

stops.step: "We all came out of Gogol's Overcoat," the line usually pinned on Dostoevsky. A clerk, a coat, and a ghost.
Nabokov teaching Gogol and Chekhov to Cornell undergrads, and taking Dostoevsky down a peg. A reading lesson by a writer.
Chekhov is what Gogol's pity looks like without the grotesque; the short story as we still write it.
Carver is the American Chekhov, and said so; he later wrote a story about Chekhov's death.

stops.t: A Swim in a Pond in the Rain
stops.step: Saunders reprints seven Russian stories and teaches them line by line, the Syracuse workshop on the page.
A former Iowa student collects Vonnegut's teaching: the rules, the jokes, the kindness toward the reader.
Irving was one of Vonnegut's students at Iowa. Owen's tiny voice and fixed fate are the lesson, grown up.

books.name: From Dresden to Copenhagen
books.why: The air war Billy Pilgrim survived, and the physicists whose work finished it, ending on a question about what Heisenberg knew.

stops.step: The meat locker, the firebombing, the twenty-three years it took to write. Start from home.
The raw material: the letter Private Vonnegut wrote home from a repatriation camp in 1945, before the jokes.

stops.t: The Fire: The Bombing of Germany
stops.step: The German side of the same sky, city by city; a 2002 bestseller that broke a long silence in Germany.

stops.t: On the Natural History of Destruction
stops.step: Sebald asks why German writers barely wrote about it. Read after Vonnegut, the question stings: the great Dresden novel came from an American POW.
Six survivors on the other side of the war, told flat and close. The same refusal to make it glorious.

stops.t: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
stops.step: How the physics got from a London street corner, where Szilard imagined the chain reaction, to Hiroshima; the scientists as characters.
Heisenberg visits Bohr in 1941 and nobody agrees what was said. Uncertainty as a moral question.
Heisenberg in his own words, after the war, on what quantum theory means. Read him knowing Copenhagen.

books.name: Pranks as Politics
books.why: Discordians, Situationists and chaos magicians all decided the joke was the revolution; the line runs through my Robert Anton Wilson shelf.

stops.c: Malaclypse the Younger & Omar Khayyam Ravenhurst
stops.step: A mimeographed religion of chaos, half joke and half koan; RAW's source code.
Discordianism blown up into a conspiracy epic: every theory is true and the reader is the mark.
Same years, same Templars, from the other side of the color line: jazz as a dancing epidemic the authorities try to cure.
The serious European version: life replaced by its image, and the prank (détournement) as the only reply.
Marcus draws the line from the Sex Pistols back through Debord, Dada and medieval heretics. A RAW book in disguise.
The Temporary Autonomous Zone: the pirate utopia as a tactic, from the same underground-press world RAW wrote for.
Morrison's comic is the whole thread as a story: Discordian cells, magic as resistance, Illuminatus! with drawings.

books.name: What Is It Like to Be
books.why: From a tick's world to an alien ocean: the question of other minds, asked of animals, plants and finally something no science can enter.

stops.t: A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans
stops.step: The tick lives in a world of three signals. Uexküll's "Umwelt" is the root idea of everything after it.
Contains "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?": you can know everything about sonar and still not know what it is like.
A philosopher goes diving and meets the octopus, a mind that evolved separately from ours.
Yong opens with Uexküll and tours the senses of other animals, as close to the bat as prose gets.
The question pushed to plants, from my own shelf: is there anything it is like to be a vine?
The limit case: a living ocean that every science fails to read. Lem's answer to Nagel, years early.

books.name: Job's Question
books.why: Why do the innocent suffer? Asked in scripture, answered with a wager, a knife, a returned ticket, a starship, and finally a joke.

stops.step: The question in its first form, and God's answer that isn't one.
"The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Pascal bets anyway.
Abraham with the knife: faith as the thing that can't be explained to anyone, Job's silence turned around.
Ivan hands back his ticket over the suffering of children. Alyosha has no argument, only kindness.
Weil on affliction from inside it: attention as the only answer Ivan can't refute.
Job retold as science fiction: a Jesuit goes to another planet sure of God's plan and comes back broken.
Satan writes home about the whole arrangement. Twain's answer is the Vonnegut answer: laugh, and be kind anyway.

books.name: The Detective Sentence
books.why: Crime fiction as a style lab: from Hammett's bare lines to Pynchon's stoned haze, the lean-to-maximal axis in one genre.

stops.step: Pure exterior: we never see inside Sam Spade's head. The lean pole at its leanest.
Chandler learned from Hammett and said so in "The Simple Art of Murder," then added the simile.
Same plain voice, now coming from the murderer. Meursault in a deputy's hat.
Almost nothing but talk; Elmore Leonard called it the best crime novel ever written.
Leonard takes Higgins's dialogue and makes it funny.
Then writes down the rules in a page: "leave out the parts readers skip."
Pynchon breaks every one of those rules and still writes a Chandler novel: the maximal pole of the same genre.

books.name: Writing Back
books.why: Four classics, each answered decades later by someone the original left voiceless. Read them in pairs.

stops.step: Huck's voice, Jim's silence.
140 years later Jim tells it, and his dialect turns out to be a performance for white ears.
The madwoman in the attic is a plot device.
Rhys gives her a name, Antoinette, and a Caribbean childhood. The attic looks different.
A white man goes up the river into Africa.

stops.t: Season of Migration to the North
stops.step: A Sudanese man goes north into Europe, and back. Conrad's journey reversed.
Meursault kills "the Arab," who never gets a name.
His brother gives him one, Musa, and answers Camus sentence for sentence. The absurd from the other side.

books.name: Is This the Simulation?
books.why: One question, 2,300 years old: how would I know if this world were staged? Each answer gets more literal.

stops.step: The butterfly dream: Zhuang Zhou can't tell whether he is a man dreaming a butterfly or the reverse, and doesn't mind.
Descartes minds very much: an evil demon could be faking everything, so what can't be faked?
1964: the demon becomes a computer and a city of simulated people who don't know it.
Dick makes it a nightmare: reality decays backward and the messages from outside come on product labels.
Baudrillard argues the copy has already replaced the world, no computer needed.
Egan runs the thought experiment honestly: a copied mind that can't tell whether it's being computed, or in what order.
The philosopher's answer: if it's a simulation, it's still real. Zhuangzi would agree.

books.name: Rules That Make Worlds
books.why: Simple rules produce endless complexity, in cellular automata and in the Oulipo's constrained novels. The same idea in math and in style.

stops.step: Conway's Game of Life: four rules, and gliders, guns and self-copying machines fall out.
Wolfram bets the universe works the same way: Rule 30 as physics. From my shelf.
Queneau, a mathematician, applies the same move to prose: one trivial anecdote run through 99 rules. He co-founded the Oulipo.
Hofstadter translates one tiny French poem 88 ways under its own constraints and writes a love letter to the Oulipo, Perec's lipogram novel included.
Perec builds a novel on a 10-by-10 apartment block toured by a chess knight; a Graeco-Latin square decides what goes in each room.

stops.t: If on a winter's night a traveler
stops.step: Calvino, an Oulipo member, writes ten first chapters on a combinatorial frame, and it reads like a thriller.

stops.t: Six Memos for the Next Millennium
stops.step: Calvino's last lectures name what the constraint was for: lightness, quickness, exactitude, multiplicity.

books.name: The Haiku Goes West
books.why: How seventeen Japanese syllables became American poetry: Bashō to Pound to Williams to the Beats, and back to Zen.

stops.t: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
stops.step: Prose travel diary broken by haiku; the source.
"In a Station of the Metro" is Pound's hokku, two lines; Imagism starts with Japanese poetry.
The red wheelbarrow: Pound's image made plain and American. Williams was Pound's college friend.
Williams, Ginsberg's mentor from Paterson, wrote the introduction. The long line, but full of Pound's "direct treatment of the thing."
Kerouac's novel of hiking with Gary Snyder ("Japhy Ryder") and Ginsberg; Kerouac writing haiku on the mountain.
Japhy speaks for himself: a Zen-trained poet writing plain, ecological poems. The haiku comes home to the land.

books.name: Kafka Creates His Precursors
books.why: Borges argued that every writer creates his own precursors: after Kafka you can see him in Zeno, Kierkegaard and Melville. This thread tests the idea.

stops.step: Zeno's paradox: the runner who can never reach the finish line. Borges's first Kafka precursor.
Another of Borges's precursors: a man under an absolute demand he can't explain. Kafka read Kierkegaard and felt it.
Borges translated it and said it defines a genre Kafka would reinvent: the office as metaphysics.
The hinge: the actual father behind the Court and the Castle, in a letter Kafka never sent.
Arrested, never charged, always in the wrong. Josef K. is Zeno's runner with a lawyer.
The paradox at full length: K. walks toward the Castle for a whole novel and never arrives.
Ishiguro's Kafka novel: a pianist who can't get to his own concert. The precursor idea run forward.

films.name: Plato's cave, six rooms
films.why: The same allegory filmed six ways, from an Italian art film to a kung fu blockbuster. Somebody wakes up and finds the walls were painted.

stops.step: Start here because Bertolucci actually has a character explain the cave, in a room with the shutters half closed. The allegory as fascism.
Three years later Fassbinder makes the cave a computer. A simulated city for German TV, from the same novel as The Thirteenth Floor.
Carpenter turns it into a B movie: put on the sunglasses and the billboards say OBEY. The cave as Reagan's America.
The cave as a 1950s sitcom, and color spreads as people start to see. The gentlest version.
Same year, same idea from the other side: the man in the cave is the TV show, and the exit is a door painted on the sky.
The maximal version, a year later. Red pill, kung fu, and the cave as a battery farm. Everything above is in its DNA.

films.name: The siege
films.why: A small group, one building, the night outside full of enemies. I keep loving this shape without noticing it is the same film.

stops.step: The template: seven men, one village, a timetable of attacks. Everyone after borrows the planning scenes.
Hawks moves the siege into a jail, made as an answer to High Noon: professionals who don't ask the town for help.
Romero swaps the bandits for the dead and the jail for a farmhouse, and nobody gets out right.
Carpenter said this was Rio Bravo plus Night of the Living Dead, and you can see the seams. A closing police station.
Carpenter remakes a film Hawks produced. Now the enemy is already inside the walls.
One building, one man, the siege flipped so the hero is the one outside the walls but inside the tower.
The lean, brutal endpoint: a tower block, floor by floor, almost no plot. Die Hard with the jokes removed.

films.name: Samurai and gunslingers trade hats
films.why: Japan borrowed the western, Italy stole it back, and then Japan and Korea took it again. A forty-year game of telephone.

stops.step: Kurosawa's lone ronin plays two gangs against each other. Hammett's Red Harvest is under it, and Hollywood westerns are around it.
Corbucci comes out of the Fistful of Dollars boom. The coffin, the mud, the machine gun. Tarantino took the name.
Corbucci again, and he lets the bad guys win in the snow. The spaghetti western at its most Kurosawa-bleak.

stops.t: Once Upon a Time in the West
stops.step: Same year, the maximal version: Leone stretches every look into an opera. The lean and the grand side by side.
Itami answers from Japan with a ramen western: a trucker in a cowboy hat teaches a widow to make noodles. The joke only works because of everything above.

stops.t: The Good, the Bad, the Weird
stops.step: Korea finishes the loop: Leone's title, Manchuria for Monument Valley, and a motorcycle in the gunfight.

films.name: The professional, stripped
films.why: Men who do one job with their hands and say almost nothing. Bresson's prison films turn into the most stylish crime films I know.

stops.step: Bresson: a prisoner, a spoon, a door. The procedure is the drama.
Becker makes its twin four years later, with real convicts digging in near silence.
Melville takes the silence and gives it a trench coat. Delon's hit man has the same patience as Bresson's prisoner.
Walter Hill brings Le Samouraï to LA: no names, no backstory, just getaways.
Mann adds the safecracking procedure and Tangerine Dream. James Caan is the professional with a home life he can't have.

stops.t: Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai
stops.step: Jarmusch openly remakes Le Samouraï with Forest Whitaker, pigeons and the RZA. The 1999 version.
Refn lifts The Driver almost whole and adds a pink font. The most maximal take on the most minimal idea.

films.name: God's lonely man
films.why: A man alone in a room, writing in a journal, waiting for grace or a gun. Paul Schrader spent fifty years remaking one Bresson film, and the trail runs straight through my Scorsese.

stops.step: The source: a sick young priest, a notebook, a parish that doesn't want him.
Bresson again, now with a thief and a diary. The last line, the touch through the bars, gets borrowed for decades.
Bergman's pastor who lost his faith. First Reformed will borrow this pastor almost whole.
Schrader's script: Travis's journal voice-over is the country priest with a cab and a .44.
Schrader and Scorsese again, twenty-three years later. The night-shift journal, now an ambulance.
Schrader directs it himself: Winter Light and the Diary fused, with a pastor and climate grief. The circle closes.

films.name: Two men in a car, the long way
films.why: The buddy movie before it became a formula, and after. Midnight Run (already seen, not on the list) is the hinge this whole thread swings on.

stops.step: Hackman and Pacino hitchhike across America. No formula yet, just two drifters who need each other.
Same year: two sailors escort a kid to prison and show him a good time first. The real grandfather of Midnight Run.
Wenders makes the German version: two men in a truck along the East German border, almost no dialogue. Same idea, other country.
Same year, the darkest take: Elaine May's hit man and the friend he's been sent to kill, one night in Philadelphia.
Walter Hill turns the engine into a genre: the cop and the con, the insults, the deadline. The template Midnight Run perfects.
Jarmusch makes it three men in a jail and a swamp, in black and white, with Tom Waits. The art-house cousin.
Shane Black brings it all back to 1977 LA. The best descendant of the whole line.

films.name: Lovers on the run
films.why: Two kids, a car, a gun, and the law a few miles behind. Godard's homage to American B movies boomerangs back into Tarantino's scripts by way of Senegal.

stops.step: Godard dedicates it to Monogram Pictures: a French punk playing at being Bogart, and the girl who turns him in.
Godard does it again in primary colors with Belmondo, and blows it up, literally.
The script was written with Truffaut in mind and offered to Godard before Arthur Penn made it. The New Wave comes home to America.
Malick makes it quiet: Starkweather as a dreamy James Dean and a girl narrating from a teen magazine.
Same year, Dakar: two lovers on a motorbike with a cow skull on the handlebars, trying to get to Paris. Godard heard in Wolof.
Lynch takes the road movie into The Wizard of Oz and wins the Palme d'Or for it.
Tarantino's script, and Tony Scott uses Badlands' xylophone theme on purpose. The romantic one.
Tarantino's story turned inside out by Oliver Stone. The maximal, TV-saturated version of everything above.

films.name: The screen talks back
films.why: Seventy years of films that saw what television would do to us, ending with a man who finds out he's the show.

stops.step: Kazan and Budd Schulberg: a drifter becomes a TV demagogue. Twenty years early on everything.
Chayefsky's sermon, the parent's angrier child. Mad as hell.
Albert Brooks moves a camera into a family's house and wrecks it. The mockumentary and reality TV, both invented as a joke.
Scorsese's answer: the fan who wants on the show badly enough to kidnap the host. De Niro at his most frightening and funny.
James L. Brooks, from inside the newsroom: the handsome anchor who doesn't understand the news versus the reporter who does and sweats on camera.
Belgium takes Real Life to its end: the film crew follows a killer and starts helping.
The last step: the camera never turns off, and the man inside is the only one who doesn't know.

films.name: The film that nearly killed its makers
films.why: Jungle shoots, river madness, and the documentaries filmed beside the disasters. The making-of is often as good as the movie.

stops.step: Herzog and Kinski on a raft down the Amazon. The template for madness on a river, on screen and off.
Friedkin remakes The Wages of Fear in the Dominican jungle and nearly sinks with it. The truck on the rope bridge is real.
Coppola takes Aguirre's river to Vietnam and the shoot goes the way the story does.

stops.t: Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse
stops.step: Eleanor Coppola's footage: the typhoon, Sheen's heart attack, Brando's weight. The film about the film.
Herzog drags a real steamship over a real mountain because the story says so.
Les Blank filmed him doing it. "I shouldn't make movies anymore. I should go to a lunatic asylum."
Herzog looks back at Kinski, including the night he planned to firebomb his house.
The one that never got made, and so never killed anyone. The madness without the jungle.

films.name: Holy fools
films.why: The innocent who walks through the world and exposes everyone around him. Chaplin to Dostoevsky to a donkey to a Washington garden.

stops.step: The Tramp, broke and kind, mistaken by a blind girl for a millionaire. The silent original.
Kurosawa moves Dostoevsky's Prince Myshkin to snowy Hokkaido. The literary holy fool, filmed.
Fellini's Giulietta Masina, a Chaplin tramp in a Roman prostitute's body. The last smile to camera is the whole thread.
Bresson said the donkey came from a passage in The Idiot. The fool with no words at all.
Ashby makes the fool a gardener whom Washington mistakes for a sage. The Vonnegut one.
The maximal, sentimental version: the fool walks through thirty years of American history. Being There with a box of chocolates.
Rohrwacher brings it back to Balthazar: a saintly farmhand out of time, and a wolf. The quiet answer to Gump.

films.name: Counting the last days
films.why: Someone learns the time is short and has to decide what the life was. Tolstoy's Ivan Ilyich keeps getting reborn in another city.

stops.step: Kurosawa's bureaucrat with stomach cancer builds one playground. Ivan Ilyich in Tokyo.
Bergman's old professor drives to an honorary degree and rereads his life on the way.
Varda's singer waits for a biopsy result, almost in real time. Paris as a waiting room.
Malle's man has chosen the date himself and spends the last day visiting friends. Camus's question, asked politely.
Fosse stages his own heart attack as a musical number. The maximal version, with Death as a woman in a veil.
Kiarostami's man drives the hills outside Tehran looking for someone to bury him. Then the camera steps out of the film.
Romania: one man passed from hospital to hospital through one night. The bureaucracy from Ikiru, now killing the patient.

films.name: Is that really them?
films.why: Real people playing themselves, reenacting their own lives, or lying about them on camera. Welles started it as a joke and it became a whole cinema.

stops.step: Welles on forgers and frauds, and he admits he's one. The essay that gives the thread its rules.
A real man who impersonated a real director reenacts his real crime, with the real victims. Kiarostami takes Welles literally.
Herzog takes Dieter Dengler back to Laos and has him act out his own escape, with hired guards.
Harvey Pekar is played by Paul Giamatti and by Harvey Pekar, sometimes in the same scene.
Linklater lets the real townspeople of Carthage, Texas tell the story around Jack Black.
Indonesian death-squad leaders reenact their killings as gangster movies and musicals. The darkest point this idea can reach.
Sarah Polley stages fake home movies of her own family's secret, and lets you take them for real.
Scorsese makes a Dylan doc with an invented filmmaker and fake interviews, and never says which. F for Fake with a guitar.

films.name: The fake band
films.why: Bands that were invented, played by actors, or so real they look like parody. The rock film as a hall of mirrors.

stops.step: The Beatles play cartoon versions of themselves. The real band acting as a fake one.
The Monkees, a band invented for TV, blow up their own image. Nicholson co-wrote it.

stops.t: The Rutles: All You Need Is Cash
stops.step: Eric Idle's fake Beatles, with George Harrison in on the joke.
Rob Reiner takes the Rutles to heavy metal and makes the template.
Woody Allen makes a straight-faced documentary about a jazz guitarist who never existed.
Todd Haynes splits a real man into six fake ones. Dylan as a fiction.
Then the real thing: a Canadian metal band whose drummer is named Robb Reiner, living Spinal Tap without the jokes.

films.name: Bird's cymbal
films.why: One story, Jo Jones throwing a cymbal at a teenage Charlie Parker, travels from a jazz biopic into the best film about obsession I know. Then it walks back through 1988, the year of three jazz films, and ends somewhere happier.

stops.step: Eastwood keeps cutting back to the cymbal flying through the air. The humiliation that made Parker.
Chazelle's teacher tells the same cymbal story to justify cruelty. The myth weaponized, played as a thriller.
Same year, another film scored by nothing but a jazz drummer, Antonio Sánchez. The drum as a nervous system instead of a weapon.
The other side of the myth: Dexter Gordon as a burnt-out genius in Paris, saved by a fan. Kindness instead of the cymbal.
Same year as Bird, and Eastwood produced it. Monk himself, spinning between tunes.
Also 1988: Chet Baker at the end, beautiful wreckage in black and white. The cost of the myth, real.
Wenders finds the old Havana players and puts them on stage at Carnegie Hall. The happy ending Round Midnight couldn't have.

films.name: The house on the hill
films.why: Kurosawa put a rich man's house above a slum. Korean cinema built a whole new wave on that view, and on the 1980s it came out of.

stops.step: The kidnapper looks up at the executive's house from the heat below. Bong has named it for Parasite.
Lee Chang-dong runs a man's life backward to 1980 and the Gwangju massacre. Korean history as the thing that ruined him.
Bong's cops in 1986, torturing suspects under military rule while the real killer walks. Same decade, other director.
Bong again: a mother turns detective to clear her son of a girl's murder.
A year later, Lee's grandmother learns her grandson took part in a girl's death. Almost the same plot, opposite temperature.
Lee goes to Murakami and class rage: the poor boy, the rich man with the greenhouses he burns.
Bong builds the house on the hill and the basement under it. The stairs do the rest.

albums.name: In tempore belli
albums.why: Six composers answer the same war, and a string quartet that formed because of one of these pieces carries it to the end.

stops.t: Quartet for the End of Time
stops.step: Start in a prison camp: Stalag VIII-A, written for the four instruments the prisoners had and premiered to the camp in January 1941.
An old man answers the bombing of Dresden and Munich with 23 solo strings; the Eroica funeral march surfaces at the end.
Fifteen years later Shostakovich is near Dresden to score a film about the firebombing, and writes this quartet in three days instead.

stops.t: Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima
stops.step: Same year. Penderecki wrote clusters first and gave them the Hiroshima title after hearing them played.
Britten and Shostakovich were close friends. Britten sets Wilfred Owen inside the Latin Mass for the rebuilt Coventry cathedral.
Vietnam, dated "in tempore belli" and played on amplified strings. A violinist heard it on the radio in 1973 and founded the Kronos Quartet because of it.
Kronos commissioned it. Reich's childhood train rides across America set against the trains running to the camps at the same time.
Kronos recorded Górecki's quartets for the same label. The middle song sets a prayer a girl scratched on a Gestapo cell wall; the war ends as a lullaby.

albums.name: Jonny Greenwood's teachers
albums.why: How the strings and the strange keyboard on Kid A came from two classical scores, and then went back into the concert hall.

stops.step: Greenwood heard this as a teenager and went looking for the ondes Martenot, the wobbling electronic keyboard all over it.

stops.t: Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima
stops.step: The other teacher: string clusters that sound like a siren made of violins.
Both lessons land here: the ondes on "How to Disappear Completely" and "The National Anthem," and Penderecki-style string smears.
His first concert piece, for the BBC, built from radio static and quarter-tone clusters.
He reused Popcorn Superhet in the score, which is exactly why it was ruled ineligible for the Oscar.

stops.t: Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima / Popcorn Superhet Receiver / Polymorphia / 48 Responses to Polymorphia
stops.step: The student and the teacher on one record, with Greenwood writing direct answers to Penderecki.
Back in the band, with a real orchestra: the col legno strings on "Burn the Witch" are the whole lineage in a single riff.

albums.name: In a Silent Way, scattered
albums.why: Everyone in the room on one Miles session went off and started their own band; follow the sidemen and you get the whole fusion decade, ending at Mingus.

stops.step: 1969: Shorter, Hancock, Zawinul, Corea, McLaughlin and Tony Williams in one room. Every next stop is somebody leaving it.
Williams walks out with McLaughlin and organist Larry Young and makes it loud. Rock volume, jazz chops.
McLaughlin's own band: violin, odd meters, a guitar that sounds like it's on fire.
McLaughlin turns the volume toward Coltrane: "A Love Supreme" and "Naima" on two electric guitars.
Hancock's exit is the spacey one, closer to Sun Ra than to the funk he'd make next.
Zawinul and Shorter's band, now with Jaco Pastorius, the bassist who made the bass sing the melody.
Jaco's own debut, with Hancock playing on it.
The sidemen reassemble around Joni: Jaco, Herbie and Wayne play the last melodies Mingus wrote before he died.

albums.name: Duke's bass line
albums.why: Mingus learned the bass from Ellington's band, got fired by Ellington, wrote him love letters, and then recorded with him; Miles closes it with an elegy.

stops.step: Jimmy Blanton turns the bass into a solo voice in 1940. A teenage Mingus is listening.
Mingus played in Duke's band in 1953 and is the only man Duke ever fired personally. Six years later: "Open Letter to Duke."

stops.t: The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady
stops.step: Mingus's big statement, a ballet scored like Ellington's suites with the shouting turned up.
Then Duke calls him: a trio with Mingus and Max Roach. Mingus walked out mid-session and Duke talked him back in.
Same year, Duke records with the other giant. The gentlest Coltrane on the list.
When Duke died in 1974, Miles made "He Loved Him Madly," half an hour of electric mourning.

albums.name: Marc Ribot's busted guitar
albums.why: One sideman's guitar sound, from Rain Dogs through downtown jazz and Cuban son to T Bone Burnett's Americana and back to Waits.

stops.step: Ribot's scraping, wrong-sounding guitar is half of what makes this record sound like a junkyard.
His day job in the same years: John Lurie's fake jazz band, the downtown New York version of Waits's junkyard.
His own first record: noise, standards and covers, the guitar finally in front.

stops.c: Marc Ribot y Los Cubanos Postizos
stops.step: He plays Arsenio Rodríguez's Cuban son, loose and loving, through a fuzz pedal.
Ribot on guitar, with Brad Mehldau on piano and Ornette Coleman on the opener. Noir songwriting in Waits's neighborhood.
T Bone Burnett hires him for the haunted Americana sound. The same guitar, now in a country record.
Back home: Ribot and Keith Richards trading guitars on Waits's last album.

albums.name: Faust, Woyzeck and the devil's cabaret
albums.why: Two old stories, the deal with the devil and the poor soldier Woyzeck, run from Stravinsky and Berg through Weill to Tom Waits and back to the cabaret.

stops.step: A soldier sells his violin to the devil, with a narrator and a seven-piece band: music theater as a busker could stage it.
Büchner's Woyzeck, the soldier ground down until he kills, as atonal opera. Hold on to this one for later.
Weill makes the same bleak view of the poor into hit songs. Note the tango.
Schnittke gives Mephistopheles a tango too, sung like a cabaret number at the moment Faust is torn apart.

stops.c: Tom Waits, William S. Burroughs & Robert Wilson
stops.s: 01. Words and music: poets, Beats, and literary records
stops.step: Waits and Robert Wilson's Faust: a man trades with the devil for magic bullets. Burroughs wrote the words.
The sister album Blood Money is Waits and Wilson's Woyzeck, so the Berg opera comes back as Weill-style songs.
The cabaret line walks into a punk club: "Brechtian punk cabaret," piano and drums.

albums.name: Jack White's record collection
albums.why: The White Stripes as a reading list: the blues and garage records he learned from, then the old singers he went back and produced.

stops.step: "Death Letter" is here. The Stripes recorded it on De Stijl.
De Stijl is dedicated to McTell, and "Your Southern Can Is Mine" is his.
The blues above, turned up until it breaks. White wrote the notes for its 2005 reissue and called it "the very definition of Detroit rock & roll."
A guitar and a drummer, no bass, playing rockabilly like punk. White calls them a key influence; the Stripes' format is here.

stops.t: I Know You Fine, but How You Doin'
stops.step: Detroit again, a decade before the Stripes, also no bass. The scene they came up in.
White pays it back: he produced this comeback for a coal miner's daughter he'd idolized.
Same move, for the queen of rockabilly, on his own label.

albums.name: From the Kitchen to the dance floor
albums.why: Arthur Russell played cello behind Ginsberg and made disco records in the same years; follow him and you reach the room LCD Soundsystem came out of.

stops.s: 01. Words and music: poets, Beats, and literary records
stops.step: Arthur Russell is on cello. He lived in Ginsberg's building and ran music at The Kitchen, the downtown avant-garde space.
The same cellist making disco. "Go Bang!" is James Murphy's Rosetta stone.
Russell alone: cello, voice and echo. The quiet side of the same person.
The DJ who played Russell's records loudest, at the club those records were made for.
Three Bronx sisters with bass, drums and congas, a Garage favorite and one of the most sampled records ever.
DFA, the label Murphy co-ran, rebuilds that sound twenty years later. "House of Jealous Lovers."
Where the line ends for me: the reunion record, all of it audible underneath.

albums.name: Manfred Eicher's cathedral
albums.why: One label, ECM, puts a medieval vocal group, a Norwegian saxophonist, Keith Jarrett and Arvo Pärt in the same reverb.

stops.step: Notre-Dame around 1200, sung by the Hilliard Ensemble for ECM.
The Hilliards again, with Garbarek's saxophone improvising over chant and Pérotin. It became a surprise hit.
Twenty years earlier Garbarek was in Jarrett's European quartet. The lean, lyrical side of Jarrett.
Jarrett alone, improvising on a bad piano. The best-selling solo piano record ever, on the same label.
The record that launched ECM's classical series opens with Jarrett playing piano on Pärt's "Fratres."
And the Hilliards sing Pärt: the line closes back on the voices it started with.
Same house sound, from Kyiv: songs sung almost under the breath.

albums.name: Bach, rewired
albums.why: One composer passed through a Soviet piano cycle, a Brazilian song, a Moog synthesizer and a NASA record; Glenn Gould is at both ends.

stops.step: Gould's two recordings, 1955 and 1981: the same piece as a young man and an old one.
A prelude and a fugue in every key. The template for the next stop.
Shostakovich judged a 1950 Bach competition in Leipzig, heard Nikolayeva win, went home and wrote his own 24.
A jazz pianist does the same thing in 2018: he plays preludes and fugues from the Well-Tempered Clavier and answers each with a piece of his own.
Bach crossed with Brazilian song: a soprano over eight cellos.

stops.s: 09. Ambient, drone and sound art: a short skim
stops.step: Bach on a Moog in 1968. Gould himself praised it in print.
Kubrick hears it and asks for Beethoven and Purcell the same way.

stops.s: 08. World: the rest of the planet
stops.step: NASA picks Gould playing the Well-Tempered Clavier to send out of the solar system.

albums.name: Dark Was the Night
albums.why: One Blind Willie Johnson recording leaves the planet, scores a Wenders film, and through Ry Cooder leads to Mali, Havana and the Sahara.

stops.step: "Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground": slide guitar and a moan, no words.

stops.s: 08. World: the rest of the planet
stops.step: Sagan's team put it on the record sent to the stars.
Cooder built his whole score for Wenders out of that one track.

stops.s: 08. World: the rest of the planet
stops.step: Cooder flies to the source of the blues, or one of them: a duet record with the Malian guitarist.
Cooder's next trip. The session was planned with Malian musicians who couldn't get visas, so it became Cuban.

stops.t: In the Heart of the Moon
stops.s: 08. World: the rest of the planet
stops.step: The same World Circuit team finishes the Malian half: guitar and kora.
North into the desert: Tuareg guitar bands, recorded outdoors.

stops.s: 08. World: the rest of the planet
stops.step: And back to American blues-rock: Dan Auerbach of the Black Keys produced it in Nashville.

albums.name: Ron Carter's bass to Thundercat's
albums.why: Miles's second quintet shows up on a Tribe record, and the line runs through Dilla and Flying Lotus to the LA jazz revival.

stops.step: Ron Carter on bass, Herbie Hancock on piano.
Tribe brings Ron Carter in to play upright bass on "Verses from the Abstract." Jazz under rap, literally.
Dilla produced for Tribe later in the 90s; this is his last record, made in a hospital bed.
FlyLo is Dilla's most devoted student and Alice Coltrane's great-nephew. Thundercat on bass, Ravi Coltrane on sax, and Thom Yorke sings a track.
Herbie Hancock comes in, the second quintet again, plus Kendrick Lamar.
The bassist's own record: funny, sad, with Michael McDonald and Kenny Loggins.
The same LA circle as a three-hour spiritual jazz record, with Thundercat on bass.

albums.name: Kool Keith to Tom Waits
albums.why: The weird wing of hip-hop passes producer to producer until it ends on an indie record with Tom Waits singing through a megaphone.

stops.step: Kool Keith starts here, already stranger than anyone around him.
Keith as a surgeon from Jupiter. The producer is Dan the Automator.
The Automator again, with Del and Kid Koala: a space opera.
Del had sung on the first Gorillaz record, which the Automator produced. Danger Mouse gets that band's next record because of this mash-up of the White Album and Jay-Z.
That next record.
Danger Mouse and Mark Linkous, with David Lynch, Iggy Pop and Vic Chesnutt.
Linkous's own masterpiece, with Tom Waits on "Dog Door."

albums.name: No Depression
albums.why: One Carter Family song named a whole movement; follow it from the high lonesome to Son Volt, O Brother and Billy Strings.

stops.t: The Carter Family on Border Radio
stops.step: The Carters' "No Depression in Heaven," 1936, sung on Mexican border radio.
The Stanleys built a lot of their repertoire from the Carter songbook and made it high and lonesome.
Jay Farrar's old band Uncle Tupelo named their first album after the Carter song, and the movement got its name from it. This is his next band.
The same idea from the other end: old-time songs written new, produced by T Bone Burnett.
Burnett again, with Welch singing and Ralph Stanley's "O Death." It sent millions of people back to the 1930s.
The source for anyone who flatpicks a guitar.
A kid who grew up playing Doc Watson songs, now playing bluegrass at jam-band length and volume.

albums.name: What Illinois is made of
albums.why: Illinois sounds like Guaraldi plus Reich plus a church band; follow those parts, then the people Sufjan made records with.

stops.step: The bossa nova soundtrack that went around the world in 1959.
Guaraldi covers it, and "Cast Your Fate to the Wind" gets him the Peanuts job. That piano warmth is all over Illinois.
The other half: pulsing mallets and clarinets. Listen to "Chicago" right after.
Produced by Daniel Smith of Danielson, the year after Michigan.
Sufjan returns the favor and plays on Smith's family band record. This is where the brass-and-choir sound came from.

stops.s: 01. Words and music: poets, Beats, and literary records
stops.step: After Illinois he throws it away for electronics and a 25-minute finale.
Muhly, who worked as Philip Glass's assistant, writes song cycles out of lists and language.

stops.c: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
stops.step: Muhly and Sufjan together, with Bryce Dessner of the National: one song per planet.
